newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sets maximum overseas territories rice quota.
newsitem.headline: EU sets maximum overseas territories rice quota.

text.p: A tariff quota limiting rice imports to the European Union from overseas countries and territories (OCTs) to 42,650 tonnes a year (January 1 to April 30) was set by the European Commission on Wednesday.
"This decision followed from a request by the Italian and Spanish authorities in response to a strong increase in rice imports from these (OCT) countries," the Commission said in a news release.
Overseas countries and territories which are not part of the EU but which have strong links and whose citizens are largely citizens of the EU were given a special tariff free concession in 1991.
"This anticipated a low level of imports of processed rice but in the past few years imports have risen to very high levels," an official explained.
"This has happened because rice has been imported into these countries in order to gain an advantage," the official added.

ACP (African, Caribbean and Pacific) countries from which rice imports benefit by only a 50 percent reduction in EU tariffs and which are limited to an annual quota of 125,000 tonnes a year have also used the loophole.
Total exports from OCTs rose from 58,000 to 192,000 tonnes in the period from 1992 to 1995 and reached 365,029 in 1996, the Commission said in its statement.

A large part of the growth came from the Dutch Indies - Curacao, Bonaire and Aruba - and these imports, through their low price and quantity, are detrimental to the EU rice sector, the statement added.

This led Italy to request the introduction of the safeguard clause on December 4 and Spain made a second request on December 10. The new tariff limit is based on a theoretical average annual quota of 163,000 tonnes between 1992 and 1995.
Of the new annual quota 4,594 tonnes are reserved for the British OCTs Monserrat and another 1,328 tonnes for the Turkish and Caicos Islands.
